clue.text: Halfwit caught flies in pile of sand

indicators.note: flies here means escapes or departs, so the letter for caught leaves the word

parts.note: a halfwit is a dunce, a slow-witted person
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A dim-witted person drops a catch and the ball flies off into a sand pile, as on a beach cricket pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flies' looks like the insects or a fielding chance but tells you C departs from DUNCE.
explanation.definitionFit: A dune is a hill or ridge of sand heaped up by the wind, typically on coasts or in deserts.

clue.text: Flapper somewhat consoles sick cider-drinking revolutionary

indicators.note: revolutionary means turning round, so the hidden letters are read backwards
somewhat means only part of these words is used, so the letters are concealed in them

explanation.surface: A twenties flapper comforts an ill, cider-swilling radical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somewhat' finds LESSICKCID in 'consoLES SICK CIDer'; 'revolutionary' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: A dickcissel is a small American sparrow-like bird, and any bird is a 'flapper' in crossword fashion, from its wings.

clue.text: Dicky learnt uranium is lacking noticeable colour

indicators.note: dicky means unsound or shaky, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: Someone shaky on chemistry has learnt that uranium has little visible colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky', British slang for faulty, signals an anagram of LEARNT plus U.
explanation.definitionFit: Neutral tones such as beige or grey have no strong hue, so they lack obvious colour.

clue.text: Commotion as American seen in Yorkshire city with bear

parts.note: Hull is a port city in Yorkshire, England
Baloo is the bear in Kipling's The Jungle Book

explanation.surface: An American visitor and a bear turn up in Hull and cause a stir.
explanation.walkthrough: HULL is a city in the English county of Yorkshire; BALOO is the bear from The Jungle Book. The pieces join in answer order, Hull first.
explanation.definitionFit: A hullabaloo is a noisy uproar or fuss, the same sort of disturbance as a commotion.

clue.text: University exercises right to be included, but it's not ready

indicators.note: to be included means placed inside, so this letter goes within the other pieces

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercises

explanation.surface: Students exercise their right to be enrolled before they are prepared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be included' puts R inside UNIPE, after UN.
explanation.definitionFit: Unripe fruit has not yet matured enough to eat, so it is literally not ready.

clue.text: One who permits suckers to get rinsed, essentially, by old rector

parts.note: lice are bloodsucking parasites

indicators.note: essentially means at its core, so take the central letters

explanation.surface: A permit-giver lets lice be washed out by an elderly clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle of 'rinsed' is NS.
explanation.definitionFit: A licensor grants a licence, formal permission for someone to do something.

clue.text: Rotten fish is sent back

indicators.note: is sent back means returned, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: a dab is a small flatfish

explanation.surface: A diner returns spoiled fish to the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is sent back' turns DAB around.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad food has gone off, so it is spoiled or decayed.

clue.text: In Irish province, Nationalist is wanting Trident

indicators.note: is wanting means is lacking, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: Leinster is one of the four provinces of Ireland

explanation.surface: An Irish Nationalist wants nuclear Trident missiles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting' suggests desire but means lacking: N leaves LEINSTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A leister is a pronged spear for catching fish, so a three-pronged one is a trident.

clue.text: Disabled beggar's topless sex party

indicators.note: topless means without its top, so the first letter is dropped

parts.note: Porgy is the disabled beggar in Gershwin's opera Porgy and Bess

explanation.surface: A disabled beggar is topless at a debauched party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disabled beggar' is a literary reference: Porgy, the crippled beggar of Gershwin's Porgy and Bess; the 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An orgy is a wild gathering featuring unrestrained sexual activity.

clue.text: Stan messes about in test

indicators.note: about here means all around, in disorder, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A man named Stan fools about during an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' signals an anagram of STAN MESSES.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessment is an evaluation or examination, so it is a synonym for a test.

clue.text: Motorboat is trapped in Corfu weir every so often

indicators.note: trapped in means one piece is held inside the other
every so often means only some of the letters, so take alternate ones from these words

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A boat gets stuck at a weir on the Greek island of Corfu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'every so often' takes the odd letters of 'Corfu weir'; 'trapped in' places the word 'is' within them.
explanation.definitionFit: A cruiser is a motor-powered boat with a cabin, used for leisure trips on rivers and coasts.

clue.text: Reportedly overprotecting young fish

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said or heard, so the spoken word is wanted

parts.note: coddling someone is overprotecting or pampering them

explanation.surface: Someone is said to be mollycoddling a young fish.
explanation.walkthrough: CODDLING (pampering) and CODLING (young cod) are pronounced the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A codling is a young cod, a common food fish, so it is a juvenile fish in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Suitable pen-friend?

definitions.meaning: as an adjective ... means fitting or in agreement with something

explanation.surface: Is this person a fitting choice of pen pal?
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means matching or appropriate; the noun is a person who writes letters regularly to another.

clue.text: Look at father and important financial figures close to agreeing — amazing!

parts.note: to eye something is to look at it
pop is an informal word for father
a PIN is the personal identification number used with bank cards

indicators.note: close to means the end, so take the last letter of this word

explanation.surface: Watch Dad and some key money people nearly reach agreement: astonishing!
explanation.walkthrough: PIN stands for personal identification number; 'figures' plays on numbers rather than people.
explanation.definitionFit: Something eye-popping is so astonishing that it makes your eyes seem to bulge.

clue.text: Hearty emotion produced in telephone call: "Lay off, that's disgusting!"

parts.note: a bell is British slang for a phone call, as in give me a bell

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: ugh is an exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: A phone call provokes a strong reaction: someone shouts to stop, it's revolting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' signals an anagram of LAY, giving YLA. 'Give me a bell' is British for 'phone me'.
explanation.definitionFit: A belly laugh is a deep, loud, unrestrained laugh, an outpouring of hearty mirth.

clue.text: Front page story: priest punches hack

indicators.note: punches means pushes through, so one piece is driven into the other

parts.note: to hack is to slash or cut roughly

explanation.surface: A headline story: a cleric assaults a journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hack' looks like a reporter in this newspaper setting but means slash. 'punches' puts P inside SLASH.
explanation.definitionFit: A splash is journalists' slang for the main story given prominent display on a newspaper's front page.

clue.text: Happen to pass former electrical store on Parisian street

parts.note: Comet was a British chain of electrical retailers that closed in 2012
rue is French for street

explanation.surface: Chance to walk past an old electrical shop on a street in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: COMET was a UK chain of electrical shops, now closed. 'to pass' echoes 'come to pass' and links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To come true is for a hope or prediction to be realised, that is, actually to happen.

clue.text: Principle covering boyfriends in flat

indicators.note: covering means wrapping round, so the first piece goes around the second

parts.note: a tenet is a principle or belief
boyfriends are men, as in her man

explanation.surface: A rule about boyfriends staying over in the flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covering' means the principle wraps round the boyfriends, splitting just before its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenement is a flat or apartment, especially one in a large, often run-down, building.

clue.text: European guided by reputation decorated in New York

parts.note: a name is a reputation, as in making a name for yourself
guided means led

explanation.surface: A European is steered by concern for their good name.
explanation.walkthrough: The spelling with one L is American, hence 'in New York'.
explanation.definitionFit: Enameled describes something coated or ornamented with enamel, the US spelling of the British enamelled.

clue.text: Shot in back procuring a toxic gas

parts.note: shot is ammunition, ammo for short

indicators.note: back means reversed, so the word is read the other way

explanation.surface: Someone is hit in the back while getting hold of a poisonous gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot in back' reads as a wound, but 'back' reverses IN to NI.
explanation.definitionFit: Ammonia is a pungent, poisonous gas made of nitrogen and hydrogen.

clue.text: Part of TV detective associated with Lewis, primarily

parts.note: Inspector Morse is the Oxford TV detective, whose sergeant was Lewis

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so take the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A role in the TV detective series featuring Morse and Lewis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'associated with' links the pieces; the surface nods to Sergeant Lewis, the partner of Inspector Morse.
explanation.definitionFit: A morsel is a small piece or portion, especially of food, so it is a part of something larger.

clue.text: Over the phone, picture best wild plant

indicators.note: over the phone means as heard, so the sound is taken, not the spelling

parts.note: picture means see in the mind and best means beat, as in to defeat

explanation.surface: A phone caller describes a photograph of a fine wild flower.
explanation.walkthrough: SEE BEAT, said aloud, matches SEA BEET.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea beet is a wild coastal plant, the ancestor of beetroot and chard.

clue.text: Run into thicket to laugh uncontrollably

indicators.note: into means going inside, so the letter goes within the other word

parts.note: a copse is a small wood or thicket
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Someone runs into the bushes in a fit of giggles.
explanation.walkthrough: To corpse is theatre slang for an actor breaking into helpless laughter on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: In acting slang, corpsing means getting the giggles and spoiling a scene.

clue.text: Layer of molluscs damaged porthole frame

indicators.note: damaged means broken up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Shellfish have damaged the frame around a ship's porthole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' signals an anagram of PORTHOLE FRAME.
explanation.definitionFit: Mother-of-pearl, or nacre, is the iridescent inner lining that oysters and other shellfish lay down inside their shells.

clue.text: Nearly learned to inject cocaine and heroin

indicators.note: to inject means to put inside, so the drug goes into the other piece
nearly means not quite all of it, so the last letter goes

parts.note: sage means wise or learned
C is a slang abbreviation for cocaine

explanation.surface: Someone almost learned how to inject cocaine and heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' cuts SAGE to SAG; 'to inject' places C after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Scag is a slang name for heroin, the opioid drug.

clue.text: Vote against regular cycling rally

parts.note: con is a vote or argument against, as in pros and cons

indicators.note: cycling means letters go round, the first one moving to the end

parts.note: regular means even, as in an even rhythm

explanation.surface: Someone votes against a regular cycling rally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' moves the E of EVEN to the end, giving VENE.
explanation.definitionFit: To convene is to gather together for a meeting, as supporters do when they rally.

clue.text: Time in therapy

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the letters are concealed in the next word

explanation.surface: A period spent in therapy.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit inside 'thERApy'.
explanation.definitionFit: An era is a long period of history, so it is a span of time.

clue.text: Prince (as he was formerly known) originally acquired uniform in red

parts.note: once means formerly, at one time

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so take the first letter of this word

parts.note: U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: The musician Prince, back in his 'symbol' era, took to dressing in a red uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls Prince's period as 'The Artist Formerly Known as Prince'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ponceau is a bright poppy-red colour, named from the French word for the corn poppy.

clue.text: After month in recession, gave angry tirade about store's termination being certain

indicators.note: in recession means going backwards, so the word is read from right to left

parts.note: Aug is the abbreviation for August

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: to rant is to deliver an angry tirade, so ranted

indicators.note: termination means the end, so take the last letter of store

explanation.surface: After a month of economic recession, someone ranted about a shop closing down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in recession' reads the month backwards; 'about' wraps the tirade round the final E of 'store', ignoring the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Guaranteed describes an outcome that is assured, bound to happen, which is what certain means.

clue.text: Long drain beginning to dry out

indicators.note: out means removed, so that letter leaves the word

parts.note: a ditch is a channel that drains water

indicators.note: beginning to means the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A long drain starts to dry out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective for the drain but is the verb, to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: To itch for something is to yearn or long for it, an idiomatic sense of feeling restless desire.
